mainEntity.name: How long does an implant-supported single tooth last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implants are designed to be a long-term tooth replacement option. Research suggests that implants can remain functional for many years, and in some cases decades, when properly maintained. However, the lifespan of an implant is influenced by several individual factors including oral hygiene standards, lifestyle choices, systemic health, and the quality of ongoing professional care. No specific lifespan can be guaranteed, as outcomes vary between patients. Regular dental assessment is the most effective way to monitor the condition of your implant over time.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally with an implant-supported single tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, an implant-supported single tooth can support normal eating once fully integrated and restored. The implant is designed to function similarly to a natural tooth root. However, in the early weeks following implant placement, your dental team will usually recommend dietary modifications to protect the healing site. For established implants, it is generally advisable to avoid habits such as chewing very hard objects, as this can place unnecessary stress on the restoration and surrounding bone.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to experience some discomfort after implant placement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of discomfort, swelling, or tenderness in the days immediately following implant surgery is common and expected. This typically settles within a week or two as the initial healing progresses. Your dental team will provide post-operative guidance and can advise on appropriate pain management. If discomfort is severe, worsening after the first few days, or accompanied by unusual swelling or discharge, it is advisable to contact your dental practice for assessment.

mainEntity.name: How often should I see a hygienist if I have a dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: The recommended frequency of hygiene appointments for implant patients varies depending on individual oral health status and clinical need. Many patients with implants are advised to attend professional hygiene appointments every three to six months, though some may require more frequent visits. Your dental team will assess your specific situation and recommend an appropriate schedule. It is important not to delay or skip these appointments, as professional maintenance is an important component of long-term implant health.

mainEntity.name: Can peri-implantitis be treated if it develops?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis, which involves inflammation and bone loss around a dental implant, can be managed, though outcomes depend on the extent of the condition and how early it is identified. Treatment typically involves professional cleaning of the implant surface, antimicrobial therapy, and improved home care routines. In more advanced cases, surgical intervention may be considered. This is why early identification through regular check-ups is important. If you are concerned about symptoms around your implant, arranging a professional assessment is the most appropriate step.

mainEntity.name: Does smoking affect my dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Smoking has been associated with higher rates of implant complications in dental research, including impaired healing, increased susceptibility to peri-implantitis, and in some cases, implant failure. This does not mean that implants are not possible for patients who smoke, but it does mean that the associated risks are higher and that particularly thorough maintenance is important. If you smoke and have a dental implant, discussing your situation with your dental team is advisable. They can provide guidance tailored to your individual circumstances.
